questions.problem:
Which of the following integers has a multiplicative inverse modulo $27?$

- $11$
- $16$
- $23$
questions.worked_solution:
An integer $a$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $n$ if and only if $a$ and $n$ are coprime, i.e., $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

With this in mind, let's examine the given options.

- $11$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $27$ since $\text{gcd}(11,27)=1.\,\,✓$

- $16$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $27$ since $\text{gcd}(16,27)=1.\,\,✓$

- $23$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $27$ since $\text{gcd}(23,27)=1.\,\,✓$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

The multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $11,$ denoted ${3}^{-1},$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
3\cdot x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,11).
$$

Note that since $\text{gcd}(3,11)=1,$ an inverse element exists and is unique up to congruence modulo $11.$

Since the modulus $n=11$ is small, we can find the inverse $x$ by computing exponents of $3$ (modulo $11$) until we get a result of $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & ≡3\cdot 3≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {3}^{3} & ≡3\cdot 9≡27≡2\cdot 11+5≡5 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {3}^{4} & ≡3\cdot 5≡15≡11+4≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {3}^{5} & ≡3\cdot 4≡12≡11+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $3\cdot 4≡1\,(\text{mod}\,11).$ Therefore, the multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $11$ is $4.$

questions.worked_solution:
First of all, notice that $\text{gcd}(50,97)=1.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $50$ modulo $97$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $50$ modulo $97$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
50\cdot x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,97).
$$

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}97 & = & 50\cdot 1 & + & 47 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 50 & = & 47\cdot 1 & + & 3 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 47 & = & 3\cdot 15 & + & 2 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 3 & = & 2\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}47 & =97-50 \\ 3 & =50-47 \\ 2 & =47-3\cdot 15 \\ 1 & =3-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =3-2 \\  & =3-(47-3\cdot 15) \\  & =3\cdot 16-47 \\  & =(50-47)\cdot 16-47 \\  & =50\cdot 16-47\cdot 17 \\  & =50\cdot 16-(97-50)\cdot 17 \\  & =50\cdot 33-97\cdot 17 \\  & =50\cdot 33+97\cdot (-17)\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result modulo $97,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}50\cdot 33+97\cdot (-17) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,97) \\ 50\cdot 33 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,97)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $50\cdot 33≡1\,(\text{mod}\,97),$ which means that ${50}^{-1}\,\text{mod}\,97=33.$

                    Computing Inverses Using Exponentiation
canonical_examples.problem: Use trial and error to compute the multiplicative inverse of $8$ modulo $15.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The multiplicative inverse of $8$ modulo $15,$ denoted $8^{-1},$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
8 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:15).
$$

Note that since $\text{gcd}(8,15) = 1,$ an inverse element exists and is unique up to congruence modulo $15.$

Since the modulus $n=15$ is small, we can find the inverse $x$ by computing exponents of $8$ (modulo $15$) until we get a result of $1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{2} & ≡8\cdot 8≡64≡4\cdot 15+4≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ {8}^{3} & ≡8\cdot 4≡32≡2\cdot 15+2≡2 &  & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ {8}^{4} & ≡8\cdot 2≡16≡15+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $8 \cdot 2 \equiv 1 \, (\textrm{mod} \:15).$ Therefore, the multiplicative inverse of $8$ modulo $15$ is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing Inverses Using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm
canonical_examples.problem: Use the extended Euclidean algorithm to compute the multiplicative inverse of $15$ modulo $86.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First of all, notice that $\textrm{gcd}(15,86)=1.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $15$ modulo $86$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $15$ modulo $86$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
15\cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:86).
$$

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}86 & = & 15\cdot 5 & + & 11 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 15 & = & 11\cdot 1 & + & 4 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 11 & = & 4\cdot 2 & + & 3 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 4 & = & 3\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}11 & =86-15\cdot 5 \\ 4 & =15-11 \\ 3 & =11-4\cdot 2 \\ 1 & =4-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =4-3 \\  & =4-(11-4\cdot 2) \\  & =4\cdot 3-11 \\  & =(15-11)\cdot 3-11 \\  & =15\cdot 3-11\cdot 4 \\  & =15\cdot 3-(86-15\cdot 5)\cdot 4 \\  & =15\cdot 23-86\cdot 4 \\  & =15\cdot 23+86\cdot (-4)\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result modulo $86,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}15\cdot 23+86\cdot (-4) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,86) \\ 15\cdot 23 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,86)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $15\cdot 23\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:86),$ which means that $15^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 86=\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}23}.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The multiplicative inverse of an integer $a$ modulo $n$ is the unique number $x$ such that

$$
a \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:n).
$$

The word "unique" in the statement above means with respect to the inequality $0 \leq x < n.$ 

For example, $x={\color{red}{4}}$ is the multiplicative inverse of $a={\color{blue}{6}}$ modulo $23$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot 4 & ≡24 & \,(\text{mod}\,23) \\  & ≡23+1 & \,(\text{mod}\,23) \\  & ≡0+1 & \,(\text{mod}\,23) \\  & ≡1 & \,(\text{mod}\,23) & .\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following: 

- We sometimes denote the multiplicative inverse of $a$ as $a^{-1}.$ So, ${\color{blue}{6}}^{-1} = {\color{red}{4}}$ in this example.

- Be careful not confuse the notation $a^{-1}$ with the reciprocal of $a.$ In this context, both $a$ and $a^{-1}$ are *integers.*

- The uniqueness of $a^{-1}$ is up to congruence modulo $n.$ For example, since ${\color{red}{27}}\equiv {\color{red}{4}}\:(\textrm{mod }23),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}27\cdot 6 & ≡162 & (\text{mod}\,23) \\  & ≡7\cdot 23+1 & (\text{mod}\,23) \\  & ≡7\cdot 0+1 & (\text{mod}\,23) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,23) & .\end{aligned}
$$

There are circumstances when a multiplicative inverse does not exist. To this end, we have the following theorem:

*An integer $a$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $n$ if and only if $a$ and $n$ are coprime, i.e., $\textrm{gcd}(a,n)=1.$*

For example:

- We saw earlier that $6^{-1} = 4$ modulo $23.$ Indeed, $\textrm{gcd}(6,23) = 1.$ Moreover, since $n=23$ is prime, *every* integer $1 \leq x \leq 22$ modulo $23$ has a multiplicative inverse. More on that in future lessons.

- In contrast, the integer $a=2$ has no multiplicative inverse modulo $14$ since $\textrm{gcd}(2,14) = 2\neq 1.$ Intuitively, multiplying $a = 2$ by any integer $x$ modulo $14$ gives an even number, and taking the result modulo $14$ (also even) will never give us $1$ (an odd integer).

tutorials.name: Finding a Multiplicative Inverse Using Trial and Error
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we wish to calculate the multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $14.$ In other words, we want to find a number $x$ such that

$$
3 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:14).
$$

Firstly, we note that since $\textrm{gcd}(3,14) = 1,$ a unique multiplicative inverse exists. 

Since the modulus $n=14$ is fairly small, one way to efficiently compute the inverse is to use trial and error. To do this, we compute powers of $3$ and take the residue modulo $14$ until we get a result of $1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & ≡3\cdot 3≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{3} & ≡3\cdot {3}^{2}≡3\cdot 9≡27≡1\cdot 14+13≡13 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{4} & ≡3\cdot {3}^{3}≡3\cdot 13≡39≡2\cdot 14+11≡11 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{5} & ≡3\cdot {3}^{4}≡3\cdot 11≡33≡2\cdot 14+5≡5 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{6} & ≡3\cdot {3}^{5}≡3\cdot 5≡15≡1\cdot 14+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,14)\end{aligned}
$$

According to the last line, we have

$$
3 \cdot {\color{magenta}{5}}   \equiv 1\qquad  (\textrm{mod}\:14).
$$

Therefore, the multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $14$ is ${\color{magenta}{5}},$ and we can write 

$$
3^{-1} = {\color{magenta}{5}}\qquad (\textrm{mod}\:14).
$$

**Note:** We could get the same result by substituting $x=1,2,\ldots, 13$ into 

$$
3 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:14)
$$

until we get the correct congruence relation. However, the exponentiation method described above typically allows us to find the solution with fewer trials since the multiplicative inverse of $a$ (if exists) must appear among the powers of $a$ modulo $n.$

tutorials.name: Using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm
tutorials.problem:
Now, suppose we want to compute the multiplicative inverse of $23$ modulo $79.$ 

Since $\textrm{gcd}(23,79)=1,$ the inverse exists. However, the modulus $n=79$ is quite big, so finding the inverse by trial and error is inefficient. So, what do we do?

To answer this, recall that Bézout's identity states that there exist integers $u$ and $v$ such that

$$
23u + 79v = \textrm{gcd}(23,79).
$$

Now, since $\textrm{gcd}(23,79)=1,$ we have

$$
23u + 79v = 1.
$$

We can find the integers $u$ and $v$ using the extended Euclidian algorithm.  

Applying the Euclidian algorithm (we'll skip over the details for now), we find that $u=-24, v = 7.$ Therefore,

$$
23 \cdot (-24) + 7 \cdot 79 = 1.
$$

To find the multiplicative inverse of $23,$ the key is to write this result modulo $79,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}23\cdot (-24)+7\cdot 79 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot (-24)+7\cdot 0 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot (-24) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot (0-24) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot (79-24) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot 55 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $23 \cdot 55 \equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:79).$ Therefore, $55$ is the multiplicative inverse of $23$ (modulo $79$).

Finally, we can express this result using the residue function as follows:

$$
23^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 79 = 55
$$

23u + 79v = \textrm{gcd}(23,79).
$$

Now, since $\textrm{gcd}(23,79)=1,$ we have

$$
23u + 79v = 1.
$$

We can find the integers $u$ and $v$ using the extended Euclidian algorithm.  

Applying the Euclidian algorithm (we'll skip over the details for now), we find that $u=-24, v = 7.$ Therefore,

$$
23 \cdot (-24) + 7 \cdot 79 = 1.
$$

To find the multiplicative inverse of $23,$ the key is to write this result modulo $79,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}23\cdot (-24)+7\cdot 79 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot (-24)+7\cdot 0 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot (-24) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot (0-24) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot (79-24) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79) \\ 23\cdot 55 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,79)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $23 \cdot 55 \equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:79).$ Therefore, $55$ is the multiplicative inverse of $23$ (modulo $79$).

Finally, we can express this result using the residue function as follows:

$$
23^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 79 = 55
$$
